Breadth vs Width Illusion

GeometryParadoxesArea
Game: Two stacks of layers look different, but both are drawn inside the same square; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the dot on the ruler, or press the buttons, to change the number of layers. Drag the green dot onto a stack to see how wide and tall it really is.

Drag the ruler dot or press the buttons for 1 to 20 layers. Focus either dot and use the arrow keys to move it.

Look for the math

The two outer stacks do not look the same size: one seems wide, the other tall. The drawing is tricking the eye, because the two stacks are built in exactly the same square.

The claim, word for word

Bogomolny's page says: Both stacks are as tall as they are wide. However our perception is affected by the apparent number of layers in the stack. That is the claim this page keeps. The logic test checks it for every layer count from 1 to 20 at thousands of canvas sizes: the body of each barrel is S units wide and S units tall, so width and height are equal every time. The rounded caps stick out by 30 units above and below, equally on all three barrels, and do not favour either direction.

How the layers are drawn

The middle barrel has one layer. The left stack has N + 1 upright lines; the i-th one sits at X0 + S/2 + round(S/2 · cos(−π + π·i/N)) and runs down the barrel. The right stack has N curved lines, the i-th one is the lower half of an ellipse whose top is at Y0 + floor(S·i/N) − 30. Both formulas, with their integer rounding, are taken from the applet's own code; the logic test compares every line and curve with a second transcription of that code, point by point, for all 20 layer counts at many canvas sizes.

Why the eye is fooled

Count the upright lines on the left and the curved lines on the right: the same number appears in two different directions. That makes one stack look broader and the other taller, even though the measuring brackets show equal sides. This is an optical illusion about how we read layers, not a change in area or length. The article credits R. N. Shepard and A. Seckel for the illusion and its references.

The original applet used a scrollbar to set 1 to 20 layers. Here the dot on the ruler and the two buttons do that job; the drawing and the claim are unchanged.

Set the layers to 1, then to 20, and put the green probe on each outer stack in turn. The brackets always read the same two numbers.
